catalog_quote: [Volk 2011:8] Phrase-Level Stress The penultimate syllable of the phonological phrase is always lengthened. [p. 17] The penultimate syllable of a phrase enjoys special status in Mijikenda. It is the locus of phrase-level stress (realized by vowel length alone) and it is also the most prominent position for the expression of high tones, as we shall see repeatedly. [p. 174] As indicated above, the penult of the phonological phrase in Mijikenda is lengthened. This, I claim, is the only effect of phrase-level stress in the language, pitch naturally being reserved for the tone system. Penultimate stress is usually explained with a trochaic foot on the final two syllables, and this is exactly what I claim for Mijikenda: every phonological phrase has a single, obligatory foot covering the final two syllables. new_statements.rule_in_words: Duruma, like the other Mijikenda dialects, has no contrastive vowel length; the penultimate syllable is predictably lengthened and carries a demarcative stress, most clearly before pause / at the end of the phonological phrase. The language is also tonal (privative /H/ vs zero): an underlying H shifts rightward within the phonological phrase and surfaces on the (lengthened) penult; the phrase-final syllable never bears H. In Volk's Duruma examples (p.391: yu-na-chi-ba:nda, yu-na-ri-ha:dza, yu-na-chi-biniki:za) length is marked on the penult of each (one-word) phrase.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Duruma. Philippson notes that in Digo (a sister dialect, not Duruma) the H is attracted to the final rather than the penult of the group; depressor (voiced obstruent) consonants restrict how far H shifts in Duruma (Volk ex. 8) but this concerns tone, not the locus of lengthening.
new_statements.domain_note: Both statements are made at the level of Mijikenda as a whole (Volk explicitly lists Duruma among the nine dialects his study covers and gives Duruma data; Philippson's own material is Giryama/Digo). The prominence is described as phrase-level/pre-pausal: Volk transcribes length only on the penult of the phonological phrase (ni-na-mala ku-gula Ngu:wo), Philippson says 'demarcative stress.. before pause'. A word in citation form is a one-word phrase and so has penultimate lengthening/stress. No source uses the term 'word stress' for Duruma specifically; the dedicated Duruma phonology (Newman & Newman 1988, SIL ms.) could not be seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted statements are framed for Mijikenda as a whole (Glottolog subgroup miji1238). Volk 2013 explicitly enumerates Duruma among the nine dialects his study (Kisseberth's recordings) covers and prints Duruma forms with penult length (p.391); Philippson's own data are Giryama (giry1241) and Digo (digo1243), and he notes Digo deviates (H attracted to the final rather than the penult). No Duruma-only phonology could be opened: Newman & Newman 1988 'Duruma phonology' (SIL ms.) is catalogued but offline.
